text:
so  then what was this  bit at the top of our convo: hm. the eyes problem. if you can already do something like render text off screen and   
  into a texture couldnt you just like render that tab into a texture  and then just      
  blast to an image. probably doesnt work like that at all but something to that effect   
  
● You've basically described the exact mechanism — the question is how much of it already
  exists. Let me check what render-to-texture machinery the engine already has.

  Searched for 2 patterns (ctrl+o to expand)

● It literally works like that — and the engine already does the hard half. The header of
  world_window.zig (the compiled-world pop-out window) states the architecture outright:

  ▎ "scene3d already renders every scene to its OWN render-to-texture (never the 
  ▎ swapchain), and drawScene is encoder-self-contained"

  So your model stage tab is already a texture. The main window never draws 3D directly —
  every scene renders into its own target, and what you see on screen is a blit of that
  texture into the composed frame. The pop-out window exists precisely because this was
  cheap: it grabs a caller-owned scene3d.DetachedTarget (a render target outside the
  per-frame pool) and blits it into a second window's swapchain. That's your "render the
  tab into a texture" — built, shipping, driving a whole OS window today.

  The "blast to an image" half is nearly as done: capture.zig has one shared pixels→PNG
  write path (its own comment: "one write path") used by both the boot-time screenshot and
  the live __capture_frame door. Today it's fed by the end-of-frame swapchain readback;
  feeding it from a texture readback instead is a standard copy-texture-to-buffer, a few
  dozen lines.

  So the eyes problem shrinks to two small pieces:

  1. Point drawScene at a background document. Since it's encoder-self-contained, it can
  render into a DetachedTarget with its own camera pose without ever touching your
  viewport — the only prerequisite is that the target document's geometry is resident on
  the GPU, which is exactly what the session-instancing slice provides. (An agent shot
  never needs to be every-frame like the pop-out window — it renders once, on demand.)
  2. Texture readback → the existing PNG writer.

  That also upgrades what shot means for agents: instead of capturing the whole editor
  window with chrome at whatever camera you happen to have, an agent gets a clean render
  of its model at its requested pose, whether or not that tab is anywhere on your screen.
  And it composes with the pop-out window for free — if you ever want to watch an agent's
  model live, the same detached target could drive that second window instead of a PNG.

  Nothing about the build list changes — this just confirms item 4 (offscreen shot) is
  mostly plumbing between two things that already exist, hanging off item 1 (session
  instancing) like everything else. The order stands: sessions → bus admission/claim →
  seat addressing → shot → skill.
